summary: A single segmental-arch stone bridge with a voussoir ring and raised keystone, coursed spandrels, four cutwaters, a cobbled deck and a coped parapet, exposing deck sockets at both approaches.
objective: Seen from about thirteen metres the bridge reads as three tiers: the arch void and the parapet line, then individual voussoirs, spandrel courses, cutwaters and cobble courses, then the raised keystone, worn coping arris and moss at the springing.
intent_signals: arch bridge over a village stream
example_prompts: Carry the village lane over the stream on a stone bridge.
I need an arch bridge whose deck I can connect a path to.
not_for: Any claim about the load capacity or construction sequence of a real bridge.

silhouette: 6 m segmental arch springing at 0.9 m and rising 1.5 m, a real void with daylight through it
parapet running the full 9.4 m length on both faces, capped 3.87 m above the river bed
four cutwaters wedged into the flow at the springings, breaking the elevation at both ends
medium: fifteen voussoirs around the arc, alternating light and dark, each a separate block with a chamfered arris
spandrel masonry sliced into 22 courses that start on the arch extrados, alternating light and dark so the joints read as coursing
cobbled deck of about 154 stones in courses across the width, each seeded in scale and rotation
projecting string course under the parapet on both faces, with two coursing bands in the parapet itself
fine: keystone raised 7 cm proud of its neighbours and lighter than the ring, with its own capping block
worn lighter arris along the parapet coping, seeded in length on each face
one slumped coping stone out of line, tilted a few degrees, the bridge's only asymmetry
moss patches at both springings where the masonry meets the water line

principles: The arch is the whole subject. Model it as separate voussoirs around a real circle and everything above it can be simple.
Slice the spandrel rather than modelling it as a solid: each slice starts on the extrados, so the void under the arch is real and the joints double as coursing.
Cutwaters and a raised keystone are the two cheapest features that tell a viewer this bridge was built rather than extruded.
implementation: Call create({ span, width, rise, springHeight, voussoirCount, approach, parapetHeight, seed }); the deck runs along X and the water passes along Z.
Join a path to deck-west and deck-east; their normals point along the deck, away from the bridge.
Place a lantern or a figure at the lantern and deck-centre sockets rather than by hand-placing world coordinates.
observable_checks: Run scripts/kit-proof.py and count features in close.png: at least two from each detail-ladder band must be visible in the frame.
The arch void is open: nothing renders between the springings below the extrados.
Two instances with different seeds re-rub the coping, move the slumped stone and re-jitter the cobbles.

known_limits: Authored creative geometry. Nothing here is a measurement of any real bridge, arch or masonry unit.
The poly budget is the triangle count observed at default parameters; a 10 m span costs about 6600 triangles.
footprint_m is the deck plan. The built bounding box is 9.5 x 4.5 m because the cutwaters project past the parapet faces.
Only a single arch is modelled. A multi-span crossing is several instances side by side, not a parameter.
Tuned against ACESFilmic tone mapping at exposure 1.0 with no post-processing.
creative_affordances: Any parameter may be pushed outside its stated range; the range is the band that was proved, not a limit.
Raise rise and shorten span for a packhorse hump, or widen width and lengthen approach for a town bridge.

defaults.rationale: A rise of a quarter of the span gives the shallow segmental arc a village bridge has, and fifteen voussoirs over that arc give a 0.47 m block that stays countable at the close proof distance.
